activities.rationale: A culture-learning orientation, one of the main approaches reviewed by Zhou et al. (2008), suggests focusing on learnable practices rather than generalised stages.

activities.title: Mapping support and participation
learnerActions: Draw a map of the people and services they interact with academically and socially
Identify gaps (for example no contact with students outside their language group, or no use of the writing centre)
Choose one gap and plan a concrete action
Report back on what happened and what they would do next
activities.intendedInsight: Academic and social networks are resources that can be deliberately built.
activities.rationale: Morita (2004) shows that participation in academic communities is negotiated and shaped by positioning, so building relationships is part of adjustment rather than separate from it.

difficulties.pattern: 'Everyone has a honeymoon and then culture shock; I'm in the shock stage now.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners narrate their experience through popular stage models and expect difficulties to pass on schedule.
difficulties.response: Present adjustment as variable and validate feelings without predicting trajectories. Do not teach the U-curve as established fact (Zhou et al., 2008).

difficulties.pattern: Limited participation in seminars is interpreted by staff or peers as lack of ability or as a fixed cultural trait.
difficulties.revealedBy: Staff references to 'quiet international students'; learners are given fewer turns or simpler roles in group work and withdraw further.
difficulties.response: Teachers and departments should explore situational reasons such as unfamiliar norms, how the learner is positioned by others, confidence and processing time, as Morita (2004) documents, and provide structured participation opportunities (prepared roles, written or online contributions). Challenge essentialising explanations wherever they arise; with learners, discuss participation choices without treating quietness as a deficit.

difficulties.pattern: Waiting until problems are severe before seeking help.
difficulties.revealedBy: First contact with tutors or services comes after a failed assessment or crisis.
difficulties.response: Introduce services early and arrange a low-stakes first contact, such as a writing centre visit set as a class task.

difficulties.pattern: Induction, peer-mentoring and social events assume full-time, on-campus students without caring or work commitments.
difficulties.revealedBy: Part-time, commuting, mature or caring students miss induction and informal networks and report not knowing about services or expectations that others learned informally.
difficulties.response: Offer induction content and support asynchronously and at varied times, and include these students' circumstances in examples. With learners, plan transition around fixed commitments and identify services available online or out of hours.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'What is one thing about studying here that is different from your previous study, and what have you done about it?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies a specific practice, describes an action taken and reflects on resources used, including prior experience.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies a difference but describes no action, or describes feelings only.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot identify a difference, or attributes all difficulty to personal inadequacy.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional courses are themselves transition spaces in which practice-learning and networks can be built; foundation is often the first move to a new education system or to studying through English, so transition is core there. UG transition spans the first year and affects first-generation, mature, part-time and commuting home students as well as international students. PGT students have little time, so early support matters most. PGR transition is materially different (isolation, the supervisory relationship and research culture) and recurs at milestones such as progression reviews. EMI students may be moving from schooling in another language, and TNE students on articulation routes (for example two years at a branch or partner campus followed by study at the home campus) make a second transition mid-degree.
reviewNotes: Review response (R5-08): the earlier note that transition also affects home, mature and part-time students has been incorporated into the description, mastery evidence, difficulties and contextNotes.

guidance.summary: Forms of address encode relationships of power and distance (Brown & Levinson, 1987), and norms vary across institutions, countries, disciplines and individuals: first-name address between students and staff is common in some settings and unusual in others. Economidou-Kogetsidis (2011) found that lecturers' perceptions of student email requests depended on pragmatic choices, not only on grammatical accuracy, which makes the framing of a message, including how the recipient is addressed, worth teaching. Teach a checking procedure (check the person's signature, profile and self-introduction; default to title plus family name when unsure; adjust when invited) rather than a single rule.

activities.title: Signature detective
learnerActions: Examine a set of real or realistic staff email signatures and profile pages
Decide how to address each person and justify the decision from the evidence
Compare decisions with peers and identify genuinely uncertain cases
Agree a default strategy for uncertain cases
activities.intendedInsight: Address choices can be based on evidence available in context, with a safe default when evidence is lacking.
activities.rationale: Treating pragmatic choices as context-dependent decisions rather than fixed rules is consistent with research on instructed pragmatic development (Kasper & Rose, 2002).

activities.title: Local norms survey
learnerActions: Compile several email openings that vary in title, name and greeting
Ask a few staff members or experienced students at their institution to rate each for appropriateness
Analyse where raters agree and disagree
Draw conclusions about local norms and about how much they vary between people
activities.intendedInsight: Perceptions of address vary among staff, so checking local practice matters and a safe default reduces risk.
activities.rationale: Economidou-Kogetsidis (2011) examined lecturers' perceptions of student emails; an informal local replication makes local norms and their variability visible.

difficulties.pattern: Using a role noun as a form of address ('Dear Teacher', 'Hello Lecturer').
difficulties.revealedBy: Emails and spoken address that use an occupational term in place of a name.
difficulties.response: Explain that in many languages an occupational title is a standard respectful address term, whereas in many English-medium academic settings it sounds unusual; offer title plus family name, or first name where invited. Make clear the choice is not rude in intent, and that where local practice uses role nouns (as in some EMI settings) they are appropriate there.

difficulties.pattern: Combining a title with a first name ('Dr Sarah') in a setting where this is unusual.
difficulties.revealedBy: Hybrid forms in emails, often from learners trying to combine respect and friendliness.
difficulties.response: Explain that in many English-speaking institutions titles combine with family names, while noting that title plus first name is normal in some regions and institutions; ask learners to check local usage.

difficulties.pattern: Discomfort with first-name address even after being invited, leading to persistent formal address.
difficulties.revealedBy: Continued use of titles after staff sign or introduce themselves with first names.
difficulties.response: Discuss that following a person's stated preference is itself respectful, while leaving the final choice to the learner; do not pressure learners to adopt informality.

diagnostic.task: Show an email from a lecturer signed 'Best wishes, Mike' above a full signature block reading 'Dr Michael Owusu, Lecturer in Economics', and ask how the learner would open a reply.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Chooses 'Dear Mike' or 'Dear Dr Owusu' and justifies the choice from the sign-off and signature block.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Chooses an acceptable form but cannot justify it.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Uses a role noun, an unexplained hybrid form, or no greeting.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners need explicit teaching and safe defaults for their destination institution. In-sessional UG and PGT learners adjust to departmental norms and revisit the topic when they meet new roles. In EMI and TNE settings, local address norms may be the expected ones (for example title plus given name, or a respectful role noun), so the target is the convention of the learner's own context rather than an anglophone default. Doctoral researchers' address to editors, examiners and external academics is handled in the research-communication topics.
reviewNotes: Statements about where first-name address is common are practice-based generalisations; teachers should check local norms.

Review response (R1-06, R1-25): pgr removed, and the edge to acu.university-structures softened, since an address form can be chosen from a signature or self-introduction without full knowledge of institutional structure.

guidance.summary: Benesch (2001) argued that EAP should not only accommodate students to existing demands but also examine and, where appropriate, challenge them, proposing 'rights analysis' alongside needs analysis; she developed it with undergraduates. For learners, this becomes the skill of distinguishing fixed from variable and negotiable conventions and making justified choices: Chang and Swales (1999) show that apparently fixed rules about informal elements are applied variably by expert writers, and Jenkins (2014) and Canagarajah (2002) show how language policies and publishing practices privilege particular norms. Teaching should balance critique with access: learners need command of dominant conventions and an understanding of where these can be questioned or negotiated, and at what cost (Ding & Bruce, 2017). For teachers, the same question of whose norms the course teaches informs course design.

activities.title: Fixed, variable or negotiable?
learnerActions: List the requirements in a current task brief, style guide or assessment criteria (a needs analysis)
For each, find out who set it, why, and whether it is assessed, regulated, variable across contexts or open to discussion (a rights analysis)
Collect evidence from exemplars, published writing in their field or a tutor to check each classification
Identify one requirement they might legitimately query, decide how they would raise it, and discuss the likely benefits and risks
activities.intendedInsight: Some academic demands are fixed and others negotiable; recognising the difference supports informed agency rather than either compliance or refusal.
activities.rationale: Benesch (2001) proposed rights analysis as a complement to needs analysis in EAP; this is a simplified learner version that works at foundation level.

activities.title: Justify a choice
learnerActions: Find a convention in their own draft where more than one option is acceptable (for example first-person use, a translated quotation, a non-default section order)
Check how writers in their field and the module guidance handle it
Make a choice and write a two-sentence rationale addressed to the marker
Exchange rationales with a peer and discuss whether the reader would understand and accept the choice
activities.intendedInsight: Choices about conventions can be reasoned about and explained, and an explained choice is read differently from an apparent error.
activities.rationale: Chang and Swales (1999) found variation in how expert writers use supposedly proscribed informal elements, which suggests that advanced writers can be taught to make such choices deliberately.

activities.title: Whose English?
learnerActions: Read a short extract on the dominance of English in publishing or in university language policy
Discuss how this affects students and scholars in different positions
Relate the discussion to a requirement in their own programme
Write a short reflection on how they will position themselves
activities.intendedInsight: The status of English and of particular national norms in academia results from history, economics and policy rather than linguistic merit.
activities.rationale: Canagarajah (2002) and Jenkins (2014) analyse inequalities in English-medium academia that learners can relate to their own situation; this activity suits PG and in-sessional groups.

difficulties.pattern: 'There is one correct way to write in English, and my job is to find the rule.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Requests for definitive rule lists; rigid application of a single model (for example a five-paragraph template or test-preparation formula) across tasks; anxiety when exemplars vary.
difficulties.response: Show variation in conventions with exemplars from the learner's own field and module, and present choices as decisions about reader and task. Acknowledge that rule-based or test-preparation instruction served its purpose in its context; the aim is to extend it, not to dismiss it.

difficulties.pattern: Critique is used to argue that dominant conventions need not be learned.
difficulties.revealedBy: Conventions dismissed as arbitrary without weighing the consequences for assessment.
difficulties.response: Stress that critique and access go together: a precise understanding of a convention is what makes it possible to negotiate it, and choices are strongest when explained to the reader.

difficulties.pattern: Module guidance says a choice is acceptable (for example first person or a quotation in another language), but individual markers penalise it.
difficulties.revealedBy: Inconsistent feedback on the same choice across markers; learners revert to the safest form regardless of what the task allows.
difficulties.response: Teachers and module teams should align guidance with marking, state acceptable variation in criteria, and avoid penalising multilingual features that do not impede meaning. Show learners how to keep a record of guidance and raise inconsistencies with a module leader or student representative.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'Your style guide says to avoid the first person, but articles in your field use "we" and "I". What will you do in your next assignment, and why?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Checks the module's guidance and assessment criteria and disciplinary practice, makes a justified choice for this task, and says how they would confirm it with the tutor if unsure.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Makes a reasonable choice but justifies it only by personal preference or by 'the rule'.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Does not recognise that the convention varies, or dismisses the guidance without considering consequences.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation: a simplified needs-and-rights analysis of the learner's own course demands (which requirements are fixed and which can be asked about). Pre-sessional: grounded in the progression task's criteria, so learners know which choices the assessment allows. In-sessional UG and PGT: choices in assessed writing, and queries through module evaluation and student representation. PGR: choices in theses and publications, connecting to the politics of English-medium publishing (pub.multilingual-scholars). In EMI and TNE programmes, learners can examine which norms come from the awarding institution, national policy or content lecturers. The teacher-facing side, examining whose norms the course itself teaches, informs course design and is not assessed in learners.
reviewNotes: Review response (R1-10): rescoped from examining the purposes of EAP (a teacher stance) to a learner skill with observable mastery, making and justifying informed choices about conventions in one's own work; audience set to 'both'.

Review response (R5-02): opened to foundation at B1+ in simplified form, and the prerequisite idn.standards-legitimacy (B2) replaced by acu.hidden-curriculum and reg.style-myths-variation so that the topic sits early rather than at depth. Recommended cross-group edges so that it feeds later work: pub.multilingual-scholars <- acu.critical-eap (soft); idn.translingual-writing <- acu.critical-eap (soft), since negotiating translingual choices with assessors builds on judging which conventions are negotiable; idn.standards-legitimacy <- acu.critical-eap (soft).
Activities are adapted for learners from largely teacher-oriented critical EAP literature; their effects have not been tested.

guidance.summary: Dafouz and Smit's (2016) ROAD-MAPPING framework analyses English-medium education through six dimensions (roles of English, academic disciplines, language management, agents, practices and processes, internationalisation and glocalisation), offering a tool for learners and teachers to describe their own context. Macaro et al.'s (2018) systematic review found EMI expanding rapidly but evidence on its benefits for language and content learning to be limited, and reported that many content lecturers do not regard language as their responsibility. EAP in EMI and TNE settings should therefore be designed around the local language ecology and actual disciplinary demands rather than imported anglophone-campus models (Jenkins, 2014).

activities.title: Mapping our language ecology
learnerActions: Use simplified ROAD-MAPPING prompts to describe language use on their programme
Compare official language policy with observed practice
Identify where English is essential and where other languages support learning
Discuss what this implies for their English learning priorities
activities.intendedInsight: EMI contexts have their own language ecologies, which determine what academic English is needed.
activities.rationale: ROAD-MAPPING (Dafouz & Smit, 2016) was designed to analyse English-medium education multidimensionally.

activities.title: Lecturer expectations interview
learnerActions: Prepare questions about language expectations for a content lecturer
Interview the lecturer, or analyse a supplied interview
Summarise what the lecturer expects regarding accuracy, terminology and participation
Compare these expectations with the assumptions of their EAP course
activities.intendedInsight: Content lecturers' language expectations may differ from those of EAP courses and are often implicit.
activities.rationale: Macaro et al. (2018) report that EMI lecturers often do not see language support as part of their role, so learners benefit from discovering expectations directly.

difficulties.pattern: 'I must sound like a native speaker to succeed in EMI.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Anxiety about accent and minor errors; reluctance to speak in class.
difficulties.response: Focus on intelligibility and disciplinary precision, and show that interaction among multilingual users of English is the norm in many EMI settings.

difficulties.pattern: Assuming that practices from anglophone campuses apply automatically in an EMI or branch-campus programme, or the reverse.
difficulties.revealedBy: Mismatched expectations about participation, assessment formats or staff roles.
difficulties.response: Investigate local practice through documents, observation and conversations with staff and senior students before generalising.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to describe how languages are used on an EMI programme they know.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes specific practices (for example lectures in English, discussion in mixed languages, assessment in English) and draws implications for language learning priorities.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Describes official policy only.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Assumes English-only use without evidence.

guidance.contextNotes: EMI and TNE provision maps onto the stages by function: pre-degree English provision as foundation or pre-sessional, and support during a degree as in-sessional; Australian and North American bridging and direct-entry programmes are pre-sessional in function. Foundation and pre-sessional courses in EMI and TNE settings can address the topic directly, and pre-sessional courses preparing students for EMI should avoid anglophone-campus assumptions such as seminar-heavy teaching. UG and PGT EMI students need discipline-specific support that reflects local practice, including large-class lecture listening and content lecturers' expectations. Students on articulation routes need to compare the practices of both campuses. As a teacher-facing principle, the analysis informs the stageEmphasis and contextNotes of the ACU and PRG domains.
reviewNotes: TNE covers diverse models (branch campuses, franchise, validation, joint and dual awards); no TNE-specific source is in the bibliography, so TNE claims are kept general.

Review response (R1-10, R1-23, R5-09): a contexts[] facet (uk-campus, emi, tne, bridging) is a schema change outside this file. Until it exists, the topic is kept with audience 'both': the learner-facing skill is mapping one's own programme's language ecology, and the teacher-facing principle is reflected in ACU and PRG domain summaries and stageEmphasis. Recommended for the LRN group: add lrn.content-through-english <- acu.emi-tne (soft), so that analysing the EMI context feeds learners' planning for content lecturers' language expectations and the topic is no longer a leaf.

guidance.summary: Brown and Levinson's (1987) model, in which the weight of a face-threatening act depends on social distance, relative power and the ranking of the imposition, gives learners a practical heuristic for calibrating mitigation, although its claims to universality and its individualist notion of face have been widely contested. Kasper and Rose (2002) review evidence that pragmatic development often lags behind grammatical development and that instruction combining awareness-raising with practice is beneficial. Economidou-Kogetsidis (2011) shows that staff perceptions of student emails depend on pragmatic choices as well as accuracy, so politeness deserves dedicated attention.

activities.title: Power, distance, imposition ratings
learnerActions: Rate a set of academic scenarios for power, distance and imposition
Predict how much mitigation each needs
Compare predictions with authentic or teacher-written messages for the same scenarios
Revise predictions and note where local norms surprised them
activities.intendedInsight: Mitigation is calibrated to the situation rather than applied uniformly.
activities.rationale: Brown and Levinson's (1987) variables provide a usable heuristic for calibrating politeness, provided they are treated as context-sensitive rather than universal.

activities.title: Noticing mitigation
learnerActions: Read several student-to-staff messages that staff have rated for appropriateness
Highlight mitigation devices, and places where mitigation is absent or excessive
Discuss why some messages were rated as abrupt and others as overly deferential
Rewrite one message at a more appropriate level
activities.intendedInsight: Specific linguistic devices make messages more or less polite, and over-mitigation also has costs.
activities.rationale: Awareness-raising followed by production practice is supported by instructed pragmatics research (Kasper & Rose, 2002); staff ratings follow the perception-based approach of Economidou-Kogetsidis (2011).

difficulties.pattern: Direct forms ('I want…', imperatives) used where English academic settings usually expect mitigation.
difficulties.revealedBy: Bare imperatives or want-statements in emails and requests to staff.
difficulties.response: Explain that many languages mark politeness mainly through honorifics, particles or verb morphology, so a structurally direct English sentence may be a faithful translation of something polite in the L1; then teach English syntactic and lexical mitigation. Do not read directness as rudeness of intent.

difficulties.pattern: Elaborate deference: long compliments, repeated apologies for writing, the purpose buried at the end.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long, highly deferential messages in which the request is hard to find.
difficulties.response: Show that excessive deference can come across as distancing or as obscuring the point; aim for clarity plus proportionate mitigation.

difficulties.pattern: 'Adding please makes anything polite.'
difficulties.revealedBy: 'Please' attached to imperatives or demands ('Please send me the answers today').
difficulties.response: Show that 'please' marks a request but does not reduce the imposition by itself; teach modal, conditional and lexical downgraders and the use of reasons.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to evaluate and rewrite: 'I need the slides from last week. Please send them today.'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies the absence of mitigation and the imposed deadline, and rewrites with a reason, a modal or conditional request form and no unexplained deadline.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Adds politeness markers but keeps the demand and deadline.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Sees no problem with the original.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: the three variables and core mitigation devices, usually taught through emails and requests. In-sessional UG and PGT: applying these to real correspondence and meetings. PGR: assumed and revisited when managing politeness with supervisors, editors and reviewers, where disagreement must be expressed while maintaining the relationship (pub.responding-reviewers). In EMI and TNE settings, local politeness norms between students and staff may differ from anglophone ones, and the target is appropriateness in the learner's own context.
reviewNotes: Critiques of Brown and Levinson's universality claims and individualist notion of face are acknowledged in the summary, but no critique is in the closed bibliography; present the model as a heuristic.

guidance.summary: Requests to staff are among students' most frequent and consequential academic speech acts. Biesenbach-Lucas (2007) found differences between native and non-native speaker students (the study's categories) in the directness of email requests to faculty and in their use of mitigating modification, and Economidou-Kogetsidis (2011) found that lecturers perceived unmitigated or imposing requests negatively even when they were grammatically accurate. Teach request structure (head act, internal and external modification) using categories from cross-cultural request research (Blum-Kulka et al., 1989), always calibrated to the imposition and to any procedure that governs the request.

activities.title: Imposition ladder
learnerActions: Rank a set of academic requests by imposition, from asking for a link to asking for a reference at short notice
Write requests at three points on the ladder
Compare modification choices with peers and with models
Identify which requests are governed by formal procedures
activities.intendedInsight: Mitigation should increase with imposition, and some requests belong in formal processes rather than personal appeals.
activities.rationale: Request research describes how modification varies with situational factors and how learners may under- or over-modify (Blum-Kulka et al., 1989; Biesenbach-Lucas, 2007).

activities.title: Request anatomy
learnerActions: Analyse student requests into opening, reason, head act, modification and closing
Identify missing or excessive elements
Rewrite one request twice, as an email and as a spoken request in person
Get peer feedback on clarity and tone
activities.intendedInsight: Requests have identifiable parts, each with a function that can be adjusted.
activities.rationale: Analysing request components follows the coding categories widely used in request research (Blum-Kulka et al., 1989) and makes pragmatic choices teachable (Kasper & Rose, 2002).

difficulties.pattern: Requests framed as needs or obligations ('I need an extension', 'You should send me').
difficulties.revealedBy: Want and need statements used as the head act in requests to staff.
difficulties.response: Teach preparatory forms ('Could you…', 'Would it be possible to…') and conditional mitigation. Do not simply ban 'I need'; a need statement with a clear reason can be appropriate. Expect these forms to develop gradually rather than all at once.

difficulties.pattern: Imposing time pressure ('Please reply as soon as possible').
difficulties.revealedBy: Urgency markers without explanation, often carried over from service or business email templates.
difficulties.response: Show how unexplained time demands increase the imposition, and teach how to signal genuine urgency with a reason.

difficulties.pattern: 'It is more polite to give all the background before I ask.'
difficulties.revealedBy: The request appears only in the final lines or is merely implied.
difficulties.response: Teach an early purpose statement followed by context, and show how busy recipients read emails. Acknowledge that context-first ordering is valued in many settings and is not wrong in principle.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write a request for a three-day extension because of illness.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Refers to the formal procedure, states the request clearly, gives the reason, mitigates proportionately and offers evidence.
diagnostic.partialResponse: States a clear request with a reason but ignores the procedure, or is clearly under- or over-mitigated.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Makes a demand without a reason or any reference to procedure.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: core request forms and the idea of imposition, practised on requests learners will actually make. In-sessional UG and PGT: real requests for meetings, feedback, extensions and references. PGR: high-imposition requests to supervisors, external researchers, data gatekeepers and editors, often across institutions, which differ materially in stakes and audience. In EMI and TNE programmes, which requests go to whom (and whether through a formal procedure) may follow local or awarding-institution rules, so learners should check them.

guidance.summary: Email to staff is a hybrid genre between letter and conversation, and student emails are judged on content, structure and politeness together. Biesenbach-Lucas (2007) and Economidou-Kogetsidis (2011) document variation in how students open, frame and close emails and mitigate requests, and Economidou-Kogetsidis shows how such features shape lecturers' perceptions. Teach email as a genre with recognisable moves (subject, greeting, identification, purpose, context, request, closing, signature) whose realisation varies with recipient and local norms, using analysis of authentic examples and rewriting.

activities.title: Inbox triage
learnerActions: Read a set of anonymised or invented student emails as if they were a busy lecturer
Decide which could be answered immediately and why
Identify what made the others hard to answer (missing information, unclear purpose, tone)
Rewrite one so that it could be answered in a single reply
activities.intendedInsight: An email succeeds when it makes the recipient's task easy.
activities.rationale: Taking the recipient's perspective helps learners see how structure and politeness affect perception (Economidou-Kogetsidis, 2011).

activities.title: Move analysis and rewriting
learnerActions: Identify the moves in several model emails
Compare openings and closings across emails to different recipients
Write an email for a given scenario
Peer-review it with a move checklist and revise
activities.intendedInsight: Emails have a predictable structure that varies with recipient and purpose.
activities.rationale: Move analysis makes the genre's structure explicit, and Biesenbach-Lucas (2007) shows variation in how students realise its elements.

difficulties.pattern: Blank or uninformative subject lines ('Hello', 'Question').
difficulties.revealedBy: Emails without a subject or with a generic one, which staff may overlook or deprioritise.
difficulties.response: Practise subject lines that include the module code and purpose, and have learners sort an inbox by subject line alone to see the effect. Do not treat a weak subject line as carelessness; it is usually unfamiliarity with how staff triage email.

difficulties.pattern: Writing as in instant messaging: no greeting, lower case, abbreviations.
difficulties.revealedBy: Messages such as 'hi can u send the slides'.
difficulties.response: Contrast channels and audiences and show how such messages may be perceived by staff. Frame this as audience adaptation, not a moral failing.

difficulties.pattern: No identifying details (full name, module, student number).
difficulties.revealedBy: Staff cannot tell who the sender is or which module the query concerns.
difficulties.response: Provide a signature template and a pre-send checklist. Do not rely on correcting individual emails after the event; a routine is more effective than repeated reminders.

diagnostic.task: Give a scenario and ten minutes to write the email.
diagnostic.strongResponse: All moves present; informative subject line; clear early purpose; proportionate mitigation; identifying details.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Clear purpose but a weak subject line, missing identification or uneven tone.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Unclear purpose, inappropriate address or an unmitigated demand.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: the core genre and its moves, using the destination institution's conventions; pre-sessional PG adds emails to prospective supervisors. In-sessional UG and PGT: revisited when writing to new roles (administrators, tutors, dissertation supervisors). PGR: revisited for emails to external academics, conference organisers and editors; correspondence with editors overlaps with pub.cover-letters. In some EMI and TNE settings, messaging apps or VLE messages replace email for routine contact (see prg.messaging-channels).

guidance.summary: Office hours and tutorials are an institutional genre with recurring phases (opening, stating purpose, discussion, closing) and a status asymmetry that students must manage. Bardovi-Harlig and Hartford (1990) found differences between native and nonnative speaker students (the study's categories) in academic advising sessions in how suggestions and rejections were made and in the use of status-preserving mitigation, and Biber (2006) describes office hours as a distinct interactive university register. Preparing specific questions and rehearsing openings, clarification requests and closings is intended to help learners use an often under-used resource with confidence.

activities.title: Office hour rehearsal
learnerActions: Prepare for a real or simulated meeting: purpose, two or three questions, materials
Role-play with a peer or teacher playing a tutor who gives brief or vague advice
Practise clarification requests and a closing summary of actions
Debrief on what worked and what to change
activities.intendedInsight: Preparation and specific questions make short meetings productive.
activities.rationale: Rehearsing interactional sequences with feedback supports pragmatic development (Kasper & Rose, 2002).

activities.title: Analysing meeting talk
learnerActions: Listen to a recording or read a transcript of an office hour or tutorial
Identify the phases and who initiates each
Note the language used to frame purpose, ask for clarification and close
Compile a short personal phrase bank
activities.intendedInsight: Meetings follow patterns that can be anticipated and prepared for.
activities.rationale: Biber (2006) documents office hours as a distinctive university register; examining it makes its patterns available to learners.

difficulties.pattern: 'Meetings with staff are only for serious problems.'
difficulties.revealedBy: No attendance at office hours; questions saved until after assessment, often by learners from systems where staff contact was by appointment for exceptional matters or where no office-hour system existed.
difficulties.response: Explain what office hours are for in the target institution and give concrete reasons to attend (checking a plan, discussing feedback). Arrange a first visit as a class task where possible. Acknowledge that arrangements differ: some institutions, including many EMI programmes, have no office-hour system, so the skill is finding out how one-to-one contact works locally.

difficulties.pattern: Arriving without specific questions or materials.
difficulties.revealedBy: Meetings end without clear outcomes; learners report that the meeting 'did not help'.
difficulties.response: Use a short preparation sheet (purpose, questions, materials, desired outcome) before each meeting. Do not treat an unproductive meeting as lack of effort; preparation for this genre has usually never been taught.

difficulties.pattern: Accepting vague advice without asking what it means.
difficulties.revealedBy: The learner agrees during the meeting but cannot act on the advice afterwards.
difficulties.response: Practise clarification and summarising moves and present them as expected, not as challenges to the tutor.

difficulties.pattern: Office hours are offered only in person at fixed times that commuting, part-time, working or caring students cannot attend.
difficulties.revealedBy: The same students never use office hours despite wanting feedback; requests for alternatives go unanswered.
difficulties.response: Staff and departments should offer bookable online or alternative slots and accept written questions in advance. Show learners how to request an alternative format politely by email.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'You have ten minutes with your tutor about your essay feedback. How will you use the time?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names specific questions about particular comments, brings the draft and feedback, and plans to summarise agreed actions.
diagnostic.partialResponse: States a general intention to 'discuss the feedback'.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Would not go, or would not know what to ask.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation: what one-to-one meetings are and why to use them. Pre-sessional: rehearsal using the destination institution's arrangements, including online meetings. In-sessional UG and PGT: real feedback tutorials, personal tutor meetings and dissertation meetings. PGR supervision meetings are covered by res.supervision. Accept multiple modes of participation: questions sent in advance, written follow-up notes and captioned online meetings may suit learners with hearing impairments, anxiety or processing differences.
reviewNotes: Review response (R5-09): office hours are treated as one local arrangement for one-to-one contact, not a universal expectation of the target context.

guidance.summary: Extenuating circumstances statements, appeals and complaints are institutional genres judged against regulations, and their success depends on procedural fit, relevant evidence and a measured tone more than on persuasion. Bhatia's (1993) analysis of professional and legal genres shows how such texts are shaped by institutional purposes and constraints, and move analysis (Swales, 1990) can help learners identify what their own institution's forms and guidance expect. Because procedures, terminology and grounds differ between institutions, teaching should always work from local regulations and signpost student advice services.

activities.title: Procedure first
learnerActions: Read their institution's extenuating circumstances or appeals policy
Identify the permitted grounds, deadlines, evidence required and possible outcomes
Turn these into a checklist
Apply the checklist to a sample case
activities.intendedInsight: The regulation defines what a statement must do.
activities.rationale: Analysing the institutional constraints on a genre reflects Bhatia's (1993) approach to professional genres.

activities.title: From narrative to statement
learnerActions: Read an emotional, unordered account of events
Select the relevant facts and put them in chronological order with dates
Link each circumstance to its effect on assessment
Rewrite in a measured register and compare versions with peers
activities.intendedInsight: Selecting and ordering facts, rather than intensifying emotion, makes a statement effective.
activities.rationale: Transforming a narrative into an institutional genre makes its moves and register explicit (Swales, 1990). This is a practice-based proposal.

difficulties.pattern: Appealing to effort or deserving ('I worked very hard on this module') rather than to permitted grounds.
difficulties.revealedBy: Statements that emphasise effort, past grades or personal need.
difficulties.response: Show the grounds listed in the regulations and explain that effort or need alone is not usually a ground.

difficulties.pattern: An accusatory or emotional tone toward staff.
difficulties.revealedBy: Statements that blame named tutors or use emotive language.
difficulties.response: Separate facts from evaluation; suggest drafting, waiting and revising, and using student advice services for support.

difficulties.pattern: Disclosing far more personal or medical detail than the process requires.
difficulties.revealedBy: Lengthy personal narratives, sometimes with sensitive details unrelated to the claim.
difficulties.response: Explain that evidence and confidentiality procedures exist; disclose what is needed to establish the circumstance and its effect.

diagnostic.task: Give a disordered case and ask which details belong in an extenuating circumstances statement and in what order.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Selects relevant, dated, evidenced facts, orders them chronologically, links them to assessment impact and excludes irrelevant detail.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Selects relevant facts but omits the link to impact or the outcome requested.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Includes everything, or focuses on effort and sympathy.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: awareness of the procedures and when to use them, since circumstances can arise during these courses and may affect progression; at B1+ the aim is recognising the procedure and producing a short, templated factual statement with support. In-sessional UG and PGT: drafting when needed, alongside student advice services. In TNE programmes the awarding institution's regulations usually govern appeals, and in EMI programmes procedures and forms may be in the local language. Teachers should not advise on live cases beyond language and should refer students to advice services.
reviewNotes: No research on student extenuating circumstances or appeal statements was found in the bibliography; guidance is practice-based.
Terminology (extenuating or mitigating circumstances, special consideration) and permitted grounds vary by institution and country.

Review response (R3-17): foundation kept and cefrStart lowered from B2 to B1+, because foundation students also face extenuating circumstances processes; at that level the focus is procedural awareness and short templated statements.
Recommended for the INT group: int.policy-processes <- prg.formal-statements (soft), since integrity appeals use the same genre moves.

guidance.summary: Apologies redress a threat to the hearer's face while threatening the speaker's own (Brown & Levinson, 1987). Cross-cultural research identifies recurring apology strategies (an explicit apology expression, an account, acknowledgement of responsibility, an offer of repair and a promise of forbearance) whose selection varies with situation and language (Blum-Kulka et al., 1989), and Kasper and Rose (2002) show these develop with exposure and instruction. In academic contexts an effective apology is usually brief, offers repair and connects to any formal process, such as absence reporting.

activities.title: Apology components
learnerActions: Analyse several apologies to staff for their components
Rate each for appropriateness and explain the ratings
Rewrite weaker examples to add repair and remove over-disclosure
Discuss which situations also need a formal procedure
activities.intendedInsight: Effective apologies include repair, not only regret.
activities.rationale: Component analysis follows the categories of cross-cultural apology research (Blum-Kulka et al., 1989).

activities.title: Spoken apology role-play
learnerActions: Role-play arriving late to a seminar, missing a meeting and missing a group deadline
Practise a brief spoken apology with an account and repair
Give and receive peer feedback
Repeat with a different relationship (peer versus tutor)
activities.intendedInsight: Spoken apologies should be brief and proportionate, and vary with the relationship.
activities.rationale: Practice across varied power and distance conditions builds sociopragmatic flexibility (Kasper & Rose, 2002).

difficulties.pattern: 'The more detail I give, the more sincere I seem.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Long accounts with personal detail and little repair.
difficulties.response: Show that brief accounts are the norm in this context and that detailed evidence belongs in formal processes, not personal apologies.

difficulties.pattern: Giving an explanation but no explicit apology expression.
difficulties.revealedBy: Messages that explain the absence but never say sorry or acknowledge the inconvenience.
difficulties.response: Teach explicit apology expressions alongside accounts and show how their absence may be read. Do not assume the learner intended no apology.

difficulties.pattern: Excessive self-criticism and repeated apologies.
difficulties.revealedBy: Multiple apologies in one message; self-deprecating language.
difficulties.response: Model proportionate apologies and reassure learners that a single, sincere apology with repair is sufficient.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to apologise, in writing or speech, to a tutor for missing a scheduled meeting.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Explicit apology, brief relevant account and concrete repair such as rescheduling.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Apology without repair, or with excessive detail.
diagnostic.gapResponse: No apology, or an account that blames the tutor or institution.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: core apology forms in speech and writing. In-sessional UG and PGT: revisited in real situations, with explicit links to absence reporting, extensions and extenuating circumstances processes. Learners should never feel obliged to disclose health, disability or family details in a personal apology; formal processes handle evidence confidentially.

guidance.summary: Asynchronous forums blend features of speech and writing; effective posts combine a clear point, support from readings and explicit engagement with peers. Hyland's (2005) model of stance and engagement provides resources for positioning oneself and addressing readers, and Coffin, Painter and Hewings (2005) analysed patterns of argument in tertiary asynchronous conferencing, indicating that sustained debate does not emerge automatically. Teaching should model replies that build on and challenge others and clarify local expectations for assessed posts.

activities.title: Reply moves
learnerActions: Analyse a forum thread for reply types (agree, extend, question, challenge, synthesise)
Identify which moves advanced the discussion
Write two replies using different moves
Peer-evaluate the replies for engagement and support
activities.intendedInsight: Replies that extend, question or challenge advance discussion more than agreement alone.
activities.rationale: Engagement resources (Hyland, 2005) help writers position themselves in relation to readers and other voices.

activities.title: Post makeover
learnerActions: Read a weak post (off-topic, unsupported or written in text-speak)
Revise it for point, support, engagement and register
Compare revisions in groups
Agree a checklist for future posts
activities.intendedInsight: Forum register sits between conversation and formal academic prose and still rewards support and focus.
activities.rationale: Explicit criteria help learners meet assessed forum expectations; Coffin et al. (2005) suggest that the quality of argument in forums varies and benefits from attention.

difficulties.pattern: Replies that only agree ('Great post, I totally agree').
difficulties.revealedBy: Threads made up of agreement with no development.
difficulties.response: Teach mitigated disagreement and extension moves and show that collegial challenge is expected.

difficulties.pattern: Posting a self-contained mini-essay that ignores other contributions.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long posts that never mention peers' points.
difficulties.response: Model dialogic engagement by naming and responding to specific peer points.

difficulties.pattern: Register that is too informal or too formal for the forum.
difficulties.revealedBy: Text-speak at one extreme, essay-style impersonality at the other.
difficulties.response: Show model posts from the learner's own course and discuss what the forum's purpose requires.

diagnostic.task: Give a short thread and ask for a reply of about 150 words.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Engages a specific peer point, adds supported content and handles agreement or disagreement collegially.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Engages peers but without support, or adds support without engaging peers.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Generic agreement or an off-topic post.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: practice on the course VLE as part of blended provision. In-sessional UG and PGT: assessed forums, particularly in online and distance programmes, where posts may carry significant marks. Asynchronous forums give time to process and draft, which can suit learners who need longer to formulate contributions, but the VLE must be accessible to screen-reader users and posting deadlines should allow for different time zones.

guidance.summary: Students now communicate through several channels (email, VLE messaging and forums, enquiry systems, group chats and collaboration platforms), each with different norms of formality, privacy and response time. Biesenbach-Lucas (2007) treats student–faculty email as a medium whose politeness conventions are less settled than those of traditional letters, and Economidou-Kogetsidis (2011) illustrates how demands for urgent replies can affect lecturers' perceptions. Teach channel choice as a decision about purpose, audience, privacy and urgency, grounded in each department's stated policy.

activities.title: Channel sort
learnerActions: Sort a set of scenarios into the channels available at their institution
Justify each choice with reference to institutional or module guidance
Compare choices with peers and resolve disagreements
Make a personal reference card for future use
activities.intendedInsight: Channel choice is part of the message and is governed by local norms.
activities.rationale: Making channel norms explicit addresses an area where conventions are often unstated and still changing (Biesenbach-Lucas, 2007).

activities.title: Waiting and following up
learnerActions: Find staff response-time statements in module handbooks or staff pages
Discuss what to do while waiting for a reply
Draft a polite follow-up to be sent after a reasonable interval
Compare follow-ups and identify what makes them appropriate
activities.intendedInsight: Response times have limits, and follow-ups need sensible spacing and mitigation.
activities.rationale: Economidou-Kogetsidis (2011) discusses time-pressure demands as a source of negative perceptions in student emails.

difficulties.pattern: Contacting staff through personal social media or messaging apps.
difficulties.revealedBy: Messages to staff on personal accounts, sometimes outside working hours.
difficulties.response: Explain institutional boundaries and the reasons for them, while acknowledging that some staff and institutions do use messaging apps as an official channel (common in some EMI and TNE settings); check local norms.

difficulties.pattern: Sending several follow-ups within hours.
difficulties.revealedBy: Chains of messages on the same query, often driven by anxiety about deadlines.
difficulties.response: Discuss reasonable response times and alternative sources of help while waiting; draft a single follow-up together.

difficulties.pattern: Sharing private information in group or public channels.
difficulties.revealedBy: Personal circumstances, marks or health details posted in forums or group chats.
difficulties.response: Distinguish public from private channels explicitly and practise deciding what belongs where.

diagnostic.task: Give six short scenarios and ask which channel the learner would use and when they would expect a reply.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Chooses channels in line with stated norms, protects privacy, and sets realistic expectations about replies and follow-ups.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Most choices appropriate, but privacy or response-time expectations misjudged.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Uses one channel for everything or chooses personal channels for staff contact.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: introducing institutional channels and their purposes at the destination institution. In-sessional UG and PGT: revisited when managing group-work channels alongside staff communication. In EMI and TNE programmes, messaging apps may be the official channel for routine contact, while formal matters still go through email or institutional systems.
reviewNotes: Channel norms are changing quickly, and no source in the bibliography addresses multichannel student–staff communication directly.
Review response (R1-06): pgr removed; doctoral researchers' multichannel professional communication is covered in research-communication topics.
Overlap with dig.digital-etiquette: that topic should focus on online presence and privacy; this topic does not depend on it, to avoid a cycle.

guidance.summary: Much academic socialisation happens in informal talk with peers and staff, where newcomers pick up tacit expectations and build the relationships through which help circulates (Duff, 2010); Morita (2004) shows that how newcomers are positioned by others shapes whether they can participate at all. Biber (2006) documents conversational features across university spoken registers, including service encounters and study groups, and Channell (1994) describes vague language as a normal interpersonal resource rather than imprecision. Teach informal interaction as learnable sequences (openings, topic development, shifts into study talk and closings) through recordings and role-play, present participation as a choice with several possible forms, and address the institutional conditions that limit access.

activities.title: Before the seminar starts
learnerActions: Listen to or read short informal exchanges set in academic places (before a seminar, in a lab, at a departmental event)
Identify how each exchange opens, keeps going and closes, and where it shifts into study talk
Practise variants in pairs using role cards that vary the relationship (classmate, lab technician, lecturer)
Note which moves felt comfortable and choose one to try in a real setting if they wish
activities.intendedInsight: Informal talk has recognisable moves that can be prepared, and moving into study talk is a normal, useful step.
activities.rationale: Making the structure of informal university talk visible draws on corpus descriptions of conversational features in university registers (Biber, 2006); the sequence is a practice-based proposal.

activities.title: Network map and one step
learnerActions: Map the people met informally on the course (peers, lab or studio colleagues, staff, support staff)
Identify one relationship they would like to develop and a setting where that could happen
Plan an opener and a possible follow-up message
Carry out the plan if they choose and report back, or discuss a supplied case instead
activities.intendedInsight: Relationships in academic communities can be built deliberately, in small steps and on the learner's own terms.
activities.rationale: Language socialisation research shows newcomers gaining access to community practices through interaction with more experienced members (Duff, 2010; Morita, 2004). Reporting is optional so that no learner is pressed into social contact.

difficulties.pattern: 'Small talk is a waste of time; I'm here to study.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners avoid informal settings and later report not knowing about opportunities, deadlines or expectations that peers discussed informally.
difficulties.response: Show how information and help circulate through informal contact, without moralising. Respect a decision not to socialise and point to other routes (study groups, peer mentoring, course channels).

difficulties.pattern: Shifting abruptly from a greeting to a demanding academic question, or staying in small talk without reaching the point.
difficulties.revealedBy: The other person seems surprised by the shift, or the conversation ends without the question being asked.
difficulties.response: Teach signalling moves for topic shifts and practise them in role-play, calibrating the question to the relationship. Do not script whole conversations; let learners build a small repertoire gradually.

difficulties.pattern: Anxiety about fast colloquial speech, humour or references in group talk.
difficulties.revealedBy: The learner stays silent in informal groups, laughs along without understanding, or leaves early.
difficulties.response: Practise clarification and backchannel moves for informal talk, normalise asking what something means, and discuss accommodation as a shared responsibility in multilingual groups. Accept listening-focused participation as legitimate.

difficulties.pattern: Departmental socials are timed, located or organised (for example in the evening or around alcohol) so that some students cannot or will not attend, and seating or group allocation keeps students within their own language groups.
difficulties.revealedBy: The same students are absent from informal events; mixed-language interaction stays low despite learners' stated wish for it.
difficulties.response: Departments and teachers vary the timing and format of events, include daytime and alcohol-free options, and design mixed groups for tasks. Do not treat non-attendance as lack of motivation.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'You arrive ten minutes early for a lab session and your lab partner is already there. What would you say, and how might you get round to asking about the report deadline?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Gives a natural opener, a follow-up question or comment, a signalled shift to the deadline question and a polite close.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives an opener and the question but no bridge between them, or a long exchange that never reaches the question.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Would say nothing, or asks only the deadline question with no opening.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: openings, topic choice, shifts and closings, practised through role-play and, where possible, with current students; this may be learners' first informal English contact with staff. In-sessional UG and PGT: lab, studio and group-work settings and relationships across language groups. PGR: lab and office culture and departmental seminars, where informal contact matters for collaboration and careers; conference talk is covered by pub.conference-participation. In EMI and TNE settings informal talk among peers often happens in shared local languages, which is a resource; informal English matters most in international cohorts and with visiting staff. Participation is a choice: accept listening-focused, small-group, online or written alternatives, and never assess personality, accent or willingness to disclose personal information. Some autistic, anxious or hearing-impaired learners may prefer predictable settings, explicit scripts or text-based channels.
reviewNotes: Review response (R1-21): added to cover informal academic interaction. No source in the closed bibliography studies small talk between students and staff directly; the guidance applies research on academic socialisation, university spoken registers and vague language, and the activities are practice-based proposals.

Recommended for the PUB group: pub.conference-participation <- prg.informal-academic-interaction (soft), since conference networking extends informal academic talk to a specialist community. grm.spoken-grammar and idn.intercultural-communication must not take this topic as a prerequisite, because it depends on them.

guidance.summary: Applications for placements and graduate roles are promotional genres: Bhatia (1993) analysed job application letters, alongside sales promotion letters, as texts whose moves establish credentials and offer evidence of suitability to a reader with criteria in mind. Competency-based questions ask candidates to narrate specific experience and draw learning from it, which connects to reflective and experiential learning (Moon, 2004), and research on clinical case presentations shows students' school-genre habits clashing with workplace genre expectations (Lingard et al., 2003). Teach the genres through analysis of real adverts and successful examples, explicit mapping of criteria to evidence, and spoken rehearsal, co-delivered with careers services where possible. Conventions differ between countries and sectors, so learners should check the target context rather than follow one model CV or letter.

activities.title: Criteria to evidence grid
learnerActions: Take a real advert and list the criteria it states or implies
For each criterion, list evidence from study, projects, part-time work, volunteering, caring or other experience
Select the strongest evidence for each criterion and draft one competency answer
Peer-check the draft for specificity, relevance to the criterion and a clear result
activities.intendedInsight: Employers assess evidence against criteria, and academic and everyday experience can both supply it.
activities.rationale: Treating the application as a promotional genre with identifiable moves (Bhatia, 1993) makes its demands explicit; widening the evidence base values the experience of mature, working and caring students.

activities.title: From experience to answer, written and spoken
learnerActions: Choose one experience and make notes on situation, own action, result and what was learned
Write a 150–200-word answer from the notes
Record a two-minute spoken version as if in an interview and compare it with the written one
Revise both for 'I' versus 'we', concrete results and relevance to the question
activities.intendedInsight: The same experience can be told as evidence in writing and in speech, and brief reflection on learning strengthens both.
activities.rationale: Structured reflection on experience (Moon, 2004) underlies competency answers; rehearsing a spoken version alongside the written one is a practice-based proposal.

difficulties.pattern: 'Talking about my own achievements sounds arrogant.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Answers credit only the team or describe tasks without saying what the writer did; every claim is heavily hedged.
difficulties.response: Show that the genre asks for evidence of one's own contribution and that accurate, specific claims are not boasting. Practise 'I' for one's own actions and 'we' for shared ones. Do not push learners towards claims they consider untrue or uncomfortable.

difficulties.pattern: Generic self-description ('hard-working, motivated and a good communicator') with no evidence.
difficulties.revealedBy: Answers that any applicant could have written; claims not linked to the advert's criteria, often copied from templates.
difficulties.response: Have learners replace each adjective with a specific example and its result, mapped to a stated criterion.

difficulties.pattern: Recruitment practices treat accent, fluency or familiarity with local conventions as proxies for ability, and some placements require local experience or unpaid time that international, working or caring students cannot easily offer.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners with strong evidence receive few interviews, or feedback about 'communication skills' that names no specific problem.
difficulties.response: Teachers and careers services make conventions explicit, ask employer partners for specific feedback, and help learners present all forms of experience. Learners can request reasonable adjustments for interviews and tests and choose whether to disclose a disability. Do not respond by drilling accent reduction.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'An advert asks for evidence of time management. What example would you give, and how would you tell it in four sentences?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Chooses a specific experience and states the situation, their own actions with 'I', a result and a brief lesson.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Chooses a relevant example but tells it generally or with 'we' throughout, or omits the result.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Gives a general self-description with no example.

guidance.contextNotes: In-sessional UG: placement and internship applications, often in the second year, co-delivered with careers services and embedded in sandwich or professional programmes. In-sessional PGT: graduate-role applications and interviews within a one-year programme, alongside the dissertation, so short, well-timed input matters. PGR: translating doctoral skills for non-academic employers (Vitae, 2010); academic CVs and research statements are covered by pub.academic-cv-bio. Conventions on CV length, photographs, personal details and cover letters differ between countries (for example UK, North American and continental European practice) and sectors, so learners check the target context. Questions about visa work rights should be referred to official guidance, not answered by EAP staff.
reviewNotes: Review response (R1-36): added as an EAP-bounded topic; occupational English and careers guidance remain out of scope. No source in the closed bibliography studies competency-based applications or graduate interviews directly, so the guidance applies genre analysis and reflective-learning research and should be checked with careers colleagues.
Overlap: pub.academic-cv-bio covers academic CVs and biographies; the two topics are left unlinked so that neither gates the other.

authorNotes: Cross-group cycle risk: acu.disciplinary-knowledge <- crt.evidence-types, acu.critical-eap <- reg.style-myths-variation, acu.emi-tne <- idn.elf, prg.informal-academic-interaction <- grm.spoken-grammar and idn.intercultural-communication, and prg.professional-applications <- wpr.audience-purpose, ges.reflective-writing and sta.self-mention. Those topics should not depend on the ACU/PRG topics that depend on them.

Orientation topics (acu.university-structures, acu.teaching-formats, acu.academic-expectations) are now entry points with no prerequisites and no soft chain between them (R1-25, R3-01). VOC and LIS are asked to drop or reconsider their soft edges from acu.teaching-formats.
Overlap: acu.academic-expectations overlaps lrn.independent-study and crt.concept. Suggest those take acu.academic-expectations as a soft prerequisite rather than the reverse.
Overlap: acu.hidden-curriculum overlaps fbk.marking-criteria and fbk.feedback-literacy. Suggest the FBK topics take acu.hidden-curriculum as a soft prerequisite.
Audience: acu.academic-literacies is teacher-facing; acu.critical-eap and acu.emi-tne are 'both' (learner skill plus teacher principle).
Gap: no topic covers student voice and representation (module evaluation, course reps, student-staff committees), which is how learners can legitimately act on acu.critical-eap. Consider adding one.
Overlap: fbk.seeking-feedback (SOCIOPRAGMATIC) overlaps prg.requests and prg.office-hours. fbk.seeking-feedback takes prg.requests as a prerequisite; no PRG topic depends on FBK.
Overlap: prg.messaging-channels overlaps dig.digital-etiquette. Suggest dig.digital-etiquette focus on online presence and privacy. PRG does not depend on it, to avoid a cycle.
prg.office-hours excludes PGR because res.supervision covers supervision meetings; res.supervision already takes prg.office-hours as a soft prerequisite.

Cross-group cycle risk: prg.forum-posts depends on sem.building-on-others and sem.agreeing-disagreeing; prg.office-hours on sem.questions-clarification; prg.messaging-channels on dig.vle; prg.requests on voc.university-terminology and grm.conditionals. Those topics should not depend on PRG topics.

Gaps: (1) spoken service encounters with professional services (library, student hub, IT desk); (2) telephone and video calls with staff; (3) giving and receiving thanks and compliments in everyday academic interaction. Informal talk and departmental networking are now covered by prg.informal-academic-interaction.
